entry:
Mental processes that deal with knowledge, including the acquisition, storage, retrieval, transformation, and use of information. Cognitive processes are a pervasive part of mental life, and many occur simultaneously. They make individuals aware of their environment and help them plan and carry out appropriate responses.

Processes are typically categorized by function. [[Perception]] organizes and interprets sensory information, such as light and sound, to construct a coherent experience of objects and events. [[Attention]] prioritizes some aspects of experience while filtering out irrelevant information. [[Memory]] is the ability to retain, store, and retrieve information, and includes working memory and long-term memory. Thinking covers reasoning, concept formation, problem solving, and decision-making. Many activities deal with language, including its acquisition, comprehension, and production. Metacognitive processes deal with information about other mental processes. Classifications also distinguish conscious from unconscious processes and controlled from automatic ones. Whether feelings and emotions qualify as cognitions is debated.

Theories of cognition differ. Classical computationalism holds that cognitive processes manipulate symbols according to formal rules, much as computers execute [[Algorithm|algorithms]]. Connectionism models the mind as a network of nodes that pass information to one another. Representationalism and anti-representationalism disagree about whether cognitive processes operate on internal representations of the world.

Cognition is studied in [[Psychology|psychology]], [[Neuroscience|neuroscience]], cognitive science, and philosophy. Some researchers study [[Cognitive development]], the growth of mental abilities from infancy through adulthood. Research focuses mostly on humans but also covers how other animals acquire knowledge and how artificial systems can emulate cognitive processes. The field has roots in antiquity and gained interdisciplinary prominence with the cognitive revolution beginning in the 1950s.

The word derives from the Indo-European root *gnō-*, 'to know', through [[Latin]] *cognōscere*, 'to learn, to understand'. It entered Middle English as *cognicioun*; the earliest documented use dates to 1447.

Geopolitical rivalry, 1947–91, between the United States and the Soviet Union and their respective allies, the capitalist Western Bloc and the communist Eastern Bloc. It began in the aftermath of World War II and ended with the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|dissolution of the Soviet Union]]. The term reflects that the two superpowers never fought each other directly, though each supported opposing sides in regional proxy wars. The rivalry also took the form of ideological and economic struggle, a conventional and nuclear arms race, the Space Race, espionage, propaganda, embargoes, and sports diplomacy. George Orwell used the phrase in 1945 as a general term; Bernard Baruch applied it to the postwar confrontation in 1947.

After 1945, when the two powers had been allies, the USSR installed satellite governments in occupied Eastern Europe, and an [[Iron Curtain]] divided Europe and Germany. The U.S. declared the Truman Doctrine of "containment" in 1947, launched the Marshall Plan in 1948, and founded [[NATO]] in 1949; the Soviet-led [[Warsaw Pact]] followed in 1955. The USSR tested its first nuclear weapon in 1949. Early confrontations included the Berlin Blockade (1948–49) and the [[Korean War]] (1950–53), which ended in a stalemate. Both powers courted newly decolonized states, many of which became Third World battlefields. The Cuban Revolution of 1959 installed the first communist regime in the Western Hemisphere, and the [[Cuban Missile Crisis]] of 1962 is widely considered the closest the conflict came to nuclear war. The [[Vietnam War]] (1955–75) ended in a North Vietnamese victory.

The USSR crushed the Hungarian Revolution in 1956 and led the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968. Relations between the USSR and China broke down by 1961. In 1972 the U.S. opened diplomatic contacts with China, and the two superpowers signed treaties limiting their nuclear arsenals during a period known as détente. Tensions rose again in 1979 with the toppling of U.S.-allied governments in Iran and Nicaragua and the Soviet–Afghan War. [[Mikhail Gorbachev]] became Soviet leader in 1985 and expanded political freedoms, which contributed to the revolutions of 1989 and the collapse of the USSR in 1991. Debate continues over the relative weight of Soviet expansion and Western intervention in causing the conflict.

Country, northwestern South America, with insular regions in North America; capital Bogotá. Officially the Republic of Colombia, it is bordered by the [[Caribbean Sea]] to the north, Venezuela to the east, Brazil to the southeast, Peru and Ecuador to the south and southwest, the [[Pacific Ocean]] to the west, and Panama to the northwest. It covers 1,141,748 sq km, has a population of around 52 million, and is divided into 32 departments. The Capital District of [[Bogotá]] is the largest city; others include [[Medellín]], Cali, Barranquilla, and Cartagena. Spanish is the official language, and Creole, English, and 64 other languages are recognized regionally.

Indigenous peoples have lived in the territory since at least 12,000 BCE; the Muisca, Zenú, Quimbaya, and Tairona developed political systems headed by caciques. The Spanish landed in La Guajira in 1499 and by the mid-16th century had colonized much of the territory, establishing the New Kingdom of Granada. Independence from the [[Spanish Empire]] was declared in 1810, and the [[Gran Colombia]] period began in 1819. The country then became the Granadine Confederation (1858), the United States of Colombia (1863), and a centralized republic in 1886. Panama seceded in 1903 with the backing of the U.S. and France, giving Colombia its present borders. The name derives from [[Christopher Columbus]].

Since the 1960s Colombia has suffered asymmetric low-intensity armed conflict and political violence, which escalated in the 1990s. Security, stability, and economic growth have improved since 2000. A 2016 peace accord led to the demobilization of the FARC, but dissident groups and drug trafficking organizations remain a security challenge.

The diversified economy is the third-largest in South America and draws on natural resources such as coffee, petroleum, and emeralds. Colombia is one of 17 megadiverse countries; its territory encompasses the [[Amazon rainforest]], highlands, grasslands, and deserts. It is a member of the UN, the WTO, the OECD, and the OAS, a NATO Global Partner, and a major non-NATO ally of the U.S.

Practice of extending and maintaining political, social, economic, and cultural domination over a territory and its people by another people, in pursuit of interests defined in an often distant metropole. Colonizers differentiate themselves from the colonized and typically organize the territory into colonies separate from the metropole rather than annexing it. In settler colonialism, settlers seek to partly or completely supplant the existing [[Indigenous peoples]], possibly amounting to genocide. The term is often used as a synonym for imperialism, though scholars distinguish them; Jürgen Osterhammel locates the essence of colonialism in the existence of colonies, which are governed differently from protectorates or informal spheres of influence.

Analogous practices occurred outside Europe, including Inca forced resettlements, Arab expansion from the 7th century that produced Arabization in [[North Africa]], and Japan's administration of Taiwan from 1895 and Korea from 1910. The concept, however, was developed mainly to describe the European empires of the modern era, which spread from the 15th century to the mid-20th century, covering 35% of Earth's land by 1800 and peaking at 84% by the beginning of [[World War I]]. Portugal, Spain, Britain, France, the Netherlands, and later Belgium and Germany pursued expansion for mercantile interests, strategic rivalry, and missionary zeal. European colonialism employed mercantilism and chartered companies and was in some cases justified by a civilizing mission, often rooted in belief in a Christian mission.

Assessments of its effects differ. Documented consequences include widespread violence, genocides, the enslavement of an estimated 12.5 million Africans in the transatlantic trade, and the disruption of Indigenous societies. Scholars have shown that variations in colonial institutions can account for variations in economic development, regime types, and state capacity. Some analyses credit colonial railways, ports, legal frameworks, and public health measures with improving institutions and living standards in some regions, and note that settler mortality shaped whether governance was extractive or inclusive. Critics stress persistent inequality and resource dependence.

[[Decolonization]] proceeded in waves, with a large wave after World War II between 1945 and 1975. Some academics use the term neocolonialism for the continuation of colonial rule through indirect means.

Visual perception produced by the activation of the different types of cone cells in the eye by light. Color is not an inherent property of matter, but perception is related to an object's light absorption, emission, reflection, and transmission. Most humans have three types of cone cells (trichromacy), sensitive to long, medium, and short wavelengths; other animals may have a different number of cone types or sensitivity to other wavelengths, as bees do to [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]]. The brain then processes the signals into sensations of hue, colorfulness, and lightness.

The [[Visible spectrum|visible spectrum]] extends approximately from 390 nm to 700 nm, with red at the longer end and violet at the shorter. Most light sources emit many wavelengths, and many more spectral combinations exist than color sensations; spectra that give the same sensation are called metamers. Spectral colors, produced by light of a single wavelength, have 100% purity. Isaac Newton named the colors of the spectrum in 1671 using a Latin word for appearance. How the continuous spectrum is divided into named colors is a matter of culture and historical contingency; the ROYGBIV mnemonic is disputed, particularly over indigo and cyan.

The physical color of an object depends on how it absorbs and scatters light. Transparent objects transmit almost all light and are perceived as colorless; opaque objects absorb or reflect it; translucent objects appear colored because they scatter or absorb certain wavelengths internally.

Colors mix additively (light) or subtractively (pigments). Color spaces, abstracted as mathematical color models, assign numbers to colors and are essential to reproduction in print, photography, monitors, and television; well-known models include RGB, CMYK, HSL/HSV, CIE Lab, and YCbCr/YUV. In art, color theory governs the harmonious use of color, including complements, color balance, and the classification of primary, secondary, and tertiary colors.

Aristotle and other ancient scientists wrote on light and color, but Newton first identified light as the source of color sensation. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe published his *Theory of Colors* in 1810, and Thomas Young proposed his trichromatic theory in 1801. Different cultures associate colors with emotions, activity, and nationality.

Icy small Solar System body that warms and releases gas when passing close to the Sun. This outgassing produces an extended, gravitationally unbound atmosphere, the coma, around the nucleus, and sometimes a tail of gas and dust blown out from the coma by solar radiation and the outstreaming [[Solar wind|solar wind]]. Nuclei range from a few hundred meters to tens of kilometers across and are loose collections of ice, dust, and small rocky particles. The coma may be up to 15 times Earth's diameter, and the tail may stretch beyond one [[Astronomical unit|astronomical unit]]. A bright comet can be seen without a telescope.

Nuclei contain water ice, frozen carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, methane, and ammonia, along with organic compounds such as methanol, hydrogen cyanide, formaldehyde, and ethanol. The amino acid glycine was confirmed in comet dust recovered by NASA's Stardust mission in 2009. Nuclear surfaces have very low albedo: the Giotto probe found that the nucleus of [[Halley's Comet]] reflects about four percent of incident light, and Deep Space 1 found that Comet Borrelly's surface reflects less than 3.0%, compared with seven percent for asphalt.

Comets usually have highly eccentric orbits, with periods from several years to potentially several million years. Short-period comets originate in the [[Kuiper belt]] or its scattered disc beyond Neptune; long-period comets are thought to come from the [[Oort cloud]], a spherical cloud of icy bodies extending halfway to the nearest star. Hyperbolic comets pass once through the inner Solar System before being flung into interstellar space.

Comets differ from [[Asteroid|asteroids]], which form no tail and are thought to have formed inside the orbit of Jupiter rather than in the outer Solar System, although main-belt comets and active centaurs have blurred the distinction. As of November 2021, 4,584 comets were known, a small fraction of a potential population in the Oort cloud of about one trillion. Roughly one comet per year is visible to the naked eye. NASA's Deep Impact blasted a crater on Comet Tempel 1, and the [[European Space Agency]]'s Rosetta was the first to land a robotic spacecraft on a comet.

The word derives from Old English *cometa*, from [[Latin]] *comēta*, from Greek *κομήτης*, 'wearing long hair'.

Medium that expresses ideas with images, often combined with text or other visual information, typically in a sequence of panels. Speech balloons, captions, and [[Onomatopoeia|onomatopoeia]] indicate dialogue, narration, and sound effects. Theorists and historians have no consensus on a single definition; some emphasize the combination of image and text, others sequentiality, mass reproduction, or recurring characters. Common forms include comic strips, editorial and gag cartoons, and comic books; since the late 20th century, bound volumes such as graphic novels and comic albums, and webcomics, have become more common. As a term, *comics* is singular for the medium and plural for works collectively.

The European, American, and Japanese traditions followed different paths. Europeans often trace their tradition to the Swiss Rodolphe Töpffer, whose cartoon strips date from as early as 1827 and the 1830s. Wilhelm Busch's *Max and Moritz* (1865) had a global impact. The medium became widely popular in Europe in the 1930s after strips and books such as [[The Adventures of Tintin]]. American comics emerged as a mass medium in the early 20th century through newspaper strips, with Richard F. Outcault's *The Yellow Kid* in the 1890s often cited as the origin; comic books followed in the 1930s, and the superhero genre became prominent after [[Superman]] debuted in 1938. Japanese comics, called [[Manga|manga]], trace their origins to as early as the 12th century; the ukiyo-e artist [[Hokusai]] popularized the term in the early 19th century, and [[Osamu Tezuka]]'s prolific work helped modern manga flourish after 1945. Historians have also proposed precedents ranging from the Lascaux cave paintings and the [[Bayeux Tapestry]] to the sequential engravings of [[William Hogarth]].

In the U.S., psychiatrist Fredric Wertham linked comics to juvenile delinquency in the 1950s. Senate hearings followed, and the industry adopted the self-regulating Comics Code Authority in 1954; its content limits are said to have delayed mature themes in U.S. comics. Underground comix and graphic novels such as [[Will Eisner]]'s *A Contract with God* (1978) later broadened the medium. Comics had a lowbrow reputation for much of their history, but toward the end of the 20th century the medium gained respect as a serious art form among the public and academics.

Viral infectious disease of the upper respiratory tract that primarily affects the mucosa of the nose, throat, sinuses, and larynx. Symptoms may appear as little as two days after exposure and include cough, runny nose, sneezing, nasal congestion, sore throat, headache, fatigue, and sometimes fever, which is uncommon in adults but common in infants and young children. A sore throat occurs in about 40% of cases, and a cough and muscle aches in about 50% each. People usually recover in seven to ten days, though some symptoms may last up to three weeks. Occasionally, those with other health problems develop [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]]. Influenza symptoms are similar but usually more severe and less likely to include a runny nose.

Well over 200 virus strains are implicated. Rhinoviruses cause up to 40% of cases and have over 100 known serotypes; [[Coronavirus|coronaviruses]], adenoviruses, other enteroviruses, parainfluenza viruses, and RSV are also common. The viral cause of 20–30% of colds is unknown. Transmission is by airborne droplets or by contact with nasal secretions or contaminated objects; rhinoviruses may survive on surfaces for over 18 hours. Risk factors include attending child care facilities, poor sleep, and psychological stress. Symptoms are mostly due to the body's immune response rather than tissue destruction by the viruses. The color of nasal mucus does not show whether an infection is viral or bacterial.

There is no [[Vaccine|vaccine]], because of the rapid mutation and wide variation of the viruses, and no cure. Prevention rests on hand washing, not touching the eyes, nose, or mouth with unwashed hands, and avoiding sick people; some evidence supports face masks. Symptoms can be treated: [[Zinc|zinc]] may reduce their duration and severity if started shortly after onset, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as [[Ibuprofen|ibuprofen]] may help with pain. [[Antibiotic|Antibiotics]] should not be used, since colds are caused by viruses, and there is no good evidence that cough medicines shorten a cold.

The common cold is the most frequent infectious disease in humans. The average adult has two to three colds a year and the average child six to eight, most often in winter. Colds have existed throughout human history.

Transmission of information, in which a source conveys a message through a channel to a receiver. The precise definition is disputed. Scholars disagree about whether unintentional or failed transmissions count, whether deliberate deception counts, and whether communication only transmits meaning or also creates it. The term can also refer to the message itself or to the field of inquiry, communication studies. It derives from the [[Latin]] verb *communicare*, 'to share' or 'to make common'.

Definitions range from broad to narrow. Broad definitions include unconscious and non-human behavior, so that animals communicate within their species and flowers signal the location of nectar to bees through color and shape. Narrower ones restrict communication to conscious interaction among humans, focus on symbols and signs, or treat the communicator's intent as central. Philosopher Paul Grice identifies communication with actions that aim to make the recipient aware of the communicator's intention. Literary critic I. A. Richards held that it occurs when one mind acts upon its environment to transmit its experience to another mind. Researchers of animal and plant communication tend to define it by observable responses and by benefit to the participants, such as for survival and reproduction.

Models of communication are simplified, usually diagrammatic overviews of its main components and their interaction. Many include a source that uses a coding system to express a message, which is sent through a channel to a receiver who must decode it. [[Claude Shannon]] and Warren Weaver characterized communication as transmission involving a source, message, encoder, channel, decoder, and receiver. Models are commonly classed as linear transmission models, in which information flows in one direction; interaction models, which add a feedback loop; and transaction models. Transactional and constitutive views reject the pure transmission view, holding that communication also shapes participants' experience by creating meaning. [[Noise]] and other barriers can disrupt the process.

Human communication is commonly classified as verbal or non-verbal. Verbal communication uses messages in linguistic form, including spoken and written messages and [[Sign language|sign language]]. Non-verbal communication occurs without a linguistic system, through [[Body language|body language]], touch, and facial expressions. Communication may also be interpersonal, between distinct persons, or intrapersonal, with oneself. Communicative competence is the ability to formulate and understand messages. Visual communication uses images, graphs, and symbols.

Non-human communication includes animal and plant communication. Animals communicate in courtship and mating, parent–offspring relations, navigation, and self-defense. Chemical communication is especially important for relatively immobile plants; maple trees, for example, release volatile organic compounds into the air to warn other plants of a herbivore attack. Most communication occurs within a species because its purpose is usually cooperation. Interspecies communication occurs mainly in symbiotic relationships, and humans engage in it when interacting with pets and working animals.

How people exchange information has changed with communication technologies, among them writing systems, mass printing, radio and television, and the internet. These advances also created new forms, such as the exchange of data between computers.

Political and economic ideology whose goal is a communist society: a classless order based on common ownership of the means of production, distribution, and exchange, with products allocated according to need. Such a society would have no private property or social classes and, ultimately, no money or state. The word derives from French *communisme*, from [[Latin]] *communis*, 'common'.

Communists often seek voluntary self-governance but disagree on the means. A libertarian socialist approach stresses revolutionary spontaneity and workers' self-management; an authoritarian socialist, vanguardist, or party-driven approach aims to establish a socialist state expected to wither away. Variants include anarchist communism, Marxist schools of thought such as Leninism and its offshoots, and religious communism. These share the analysis that the existing order stems from capitalism, in which the proletariat, who sell their labor power, and the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production and profit from employing them, stand in an exploitative relationship that only social revolution can resolve.

Modern communism grew out of the 19th-century European socialist movement, which argued that capitalism caused the misery of urban factory workers. In 1848 [[Karl Marx]] and Friedrich Engels offered a new definition in *The Communist Manifesto*. Communist governments espousing Marxism–Leninism came to power first in the Soviet Union with the 1917 Russian Revolution, and after World War II in Eastern Europe, Asia, and elsewhere, including China under Mao Zedong (1949) and Cuba (1959). By the 1920s communism and social democracy were the two dominant types of socialism.

For much of the 20th century more than one-third of the world's population lived under Communist governments, characterized by one-party rule, rejection of private property and capitalism, state control of the economy and mass media, restrictions on freedom of religion, and suppression of opposition. Supporters and critics assess the record differently: some regimes achieved rapid industrialization or literacy gains, while critics point to repression, forced labor, and famines. Mass killings under communist regimes and their mortality figures remain controversial and debated. Several scholars argue that the Soviet economic model functioned in practice as state capitalism.

After the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union]] in 1991, many governments abolished Communist rule. Remaining Communist governments include China, Cuba, Laos, North Korea, and Vietnam; except for North Korea, these have allowed more economic competition while keeping one-party rule. The decline of communism has been attributed to economic inefficiency, authoritarianism, and bureaucracy. From the 1990s many Communist parties adopted democratic principles and share power with others in government.
